Select the zone your scheduler evaluates in — the server’s zone for crontab, UTC for GitHub Actions and EventBridge rules, spec.timeZone for Kubernetes. Compare the times with your local time column, and scroll the run list across the next daylight-saving change if the job runs at night.

Most failing cron jobs have a correct schedule and a broken command. Cron runs with a minimal environment: a short PATH, no shell profile and often a different user. Test with the same conditions, for example sudo -u www-data env -i /bin/sh -c 'your-command', and use absolute paths for every program and file.
Temporarily schedule the job a couple of minutes ahead, or every minute with * * * * *, and watch it run. Remove the temporary schedule afterwards.

Redirect output to a file with >> /var/log/myjob.log 2>&1 so errors are not lost. On Debian and Ubuntu, cron’s own log is in /var/log/syslog (grep CRON); on RHEL-based systems it is /var/log/cron, and on systemd hosts journalctl -u cron or -u crond. In Kubernetes, check kubectl get jobs and the logs of the pods a CronJob created.

faq.q: How can I run a cron job immediately to test it?
faq.a: Run the command directly in a shell with the same user and environment. In Kubernetes use kubectl create job --from=cronjob/NAME test-run.

faq.q: Can I trigger a GitHub Actions scheduled workflow manually?
faq.a: Yes, if you add a workflow_dispatch trigger next to schedule. It then gets a Run workflow button.

faq.q: Why does my script work in the terminal but not from cron?
faq.a: Usually PATH, environment variables or the working directory differ. Use absolute paths and set needed variables at the top of the crontab.

faq.q: How do I know the next time my cron job will run?
faq.a: Paste the expression into the explainer on this page; it lists the next 10 run times in any time zone.

linux-crontab-guide.name: Linux crontab guide
linux-crontab-guide.title: Linux Crontab Guide: Edit, List and Debug Jobs
linux-crontab-guide.description: How to use crontab -e, -l and -r, user vs system crontabs, environment variables, output and logs, and why a cron job silently fails.
linux-crontab-guide.h1: Linux crontab guide: edit, list and debug
linux-crontab-guide.intro: Crontab is the simplest way to schedule recurring jobs on Linux. This guide covers the commands you use day to day and the pitfalls that make jobs fail silently.

p: crontab -e opens your personal crontab in the default editor and installs it when you save. crontab -l prints it, and crontab -r deletes it without asking — a common accident, so keep a copy with crontab -l > crontab.bak. As root, crontab -u alice -e edits another user’s table.
Each line is a schedule and a command: 0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh. Lines starting with # are comments. The file must end with a newline, otherwise the last job may be ignored.

Personal crontabs live in /var/spool/cron and run as their owner. System-wide jobs go in /etc/crontab or files in /etc/cron.d/, which have an extra field for the user: 0 3 * * * root /usr/local/bin/backup.sh. Scripts dropped into /etc/cron.hourly, cron.daily, cron.weekly and cron.monthly run via run-parts or anacron at times defined by the system.

Cron starts jobs with a minimal environment — typically PATH=/usr/bin:/bin and the user’s home directory. Set variables at the top of the crontab (PATH=…, SHELL=/bin/bash, MAILTO=you@example.com) or use absolute paths everywhere.

Output is mailed to the owner if a mail system is configured and is otherwise lost, so redirect it: >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1. In the command part, % is special and becomes a newline; escape it as \% when calling date +\%F, for example.

sections.h: Debugging a job that does not run
p: Check that the cron service is running (systemctl status cron or crond), look for the job in the logs (grep CRON /var/log/syslog, /var/log/cron or journalctl), make sure the script is executable and has a shebang line, and run it by hand with env -i to reproduce the bare environment. Finally, paste the schedule into the explainer to confirm when it is due.

faq.q: Where are crontab files stored?
faq.a: User crontabs are in /var/spool/cron/crontabs (Debian, Ubuntu) or /var/spool/cron (RHEL, Fedora). Edit them with crontab -e rather than directly.

faq.q: Do I need to restart cron after editing?
faq.a: No. crontab -e signals the daemon, and cron also re-reads changed files every minute.

faq.q: How do I run a cron job as root?
faq.a: Use sudo crontab -e, or add a line with the user field root to /etc/crontab or a file in /etc/cron.d/.

faq.q: How do I stop cron from sending e-mails?
faq.a: Set MAILTO="" at the top of the crontab, or redirect the job’s output to a file or /dev/null.

faq.q: What does @reboot do?
faq.a: It runs the command once when the cron daemon starts, typically at boot. It has no recurring schedule.

cron-every-n-minutes.name: Cron every N minutes
cron-every-n-minutes.title: How to Run Cron Every N Minutes (*/n Patterns)
cron-every-n-minutes.description: Cron expressions for every 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 and 45 minutes, why */7 and */45 drift at the hour, and how to offset start times.
cron-every-n-minutes.h1: How to run a cron job every N minutes
cron-every-n-minutes.intro: Use */n in the minute field: */5 * * * * runs every five minutes. It works perfectly for some values of n and surprisingly for others. Here is why, and what to do about it.

p: */n in the minute field means every nth minute starting at 0, within each hour. */2 runs at :00, :02, :04 …; */10 at :00, :10, :20, :30, :40, :50; */30 at :00 and :30. Each value links to a ready-made page below, with the expression for every dialect.

The step restarts at the top of every hour. That is invisible when n divides 60 — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30 — but not otherwise. */7 runs at :00, :07 … :49, :56 and then :00 again, a gap of only 4 minutes. */45 runs at :00 and :45, alternating 45- and 15-minute gaps.
For a true 45- or 90-minute rhythm, cron alone is the wrong tool. Use AWS rate(45 minutes), a systemd timer with OnUnitActiveSec=45min, or let a frequent job check how long ago it last did its work.

To start somewhere other than :00, write a range with a step: 3-59/5 runs at :03, :08, :13 … and keeps clear of the many jobs that fire on round minutes. On a server with several five-minute jobs, giving each a different offset smooths CPU and network spikes.

Crontab and Kubernetes go down to every minute. GitHub Actions accepts */1 but will not run more often than every 5 minutes, and runs can be delayed under load. AWS EventBridge supports both cron(0/5 * * * ? *) and the simpler rate(5 minutes). For sub-minute intervals you need a seconds-capable dialect.

faq.q: What is the cron expression for every 5 minutes?
faq.a: */5 * * * * in crontab, 0 */5 * * * ? in Quartz and cron(*/5 * * * ? *) in AWS.

faq.q: Is */5 the same as 0-59/5?
faq.a: Yes. Both start at minute 0 and take every fifth minute.

faq.q: How do I run a job every 90 minutes?
faq.a: Cron cannot do it with one line. Use two entries — 0 0-21/3 * * * and 30 1-22/3 * * * — or a timer-based scheduler.

faq.q: Does */n count from when the cron job was created?
faq.a: No. It counts from minute 0 of each hour. Only rate-style schedules, such as AWS rate(), count from creation time.

aws-rate-vs-cron.name: AWS rate() vs cron()
aws-rate-vs-cron.title: AWS EventBridge rate() vs cron(): When to Use Each
aws-rate-vs-cron.description: Compare AWS EventBridge rate and cron expressions: syntax, the year field, the ? rule, UTC, minimum intervals and EventBridge Scheduler.
aws-rate-vs-cron.intro: EventBridge offers two ways to describe a schedule. rate() says how often; cron() says exactly when. Picking the right one avoids awkward expressions and surprising start times.

p: A rate expression is rate(value unit), where the unit is minute(s), hour(s) or day(s): rate(5 minutes), rate(1 hour), rate(7 days). Use the singular unit for a value of 1 — rate(1 minute) — and the plural otherwise, or the rule is rejected.

The interval counts from when the rule or schedule was created, not from the clock. rate(1 hour) created at 10:17 fires at 11:17, 12:17 and so on. That is ideal for “every N” tasks where the exact minute does not matter, including intervals cron cannot express, such as rate(45 minutes) or rate(90 minutes).

A cron expression has six fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week and year, wrapped in cron(...). For example cron(0 8 ? * MON-FRI *) is 08:00 on weekdays. As in Quartz, one day field must be ?, weekdays are numbered 1 = Sunday to 7 = Saturday, and L, W and # are supported.
Use cron() whenever the time of day or the calendar matters: daily reports, business days only, the last day of the month, or a one-off year.

Classic EventBridge rules evaluate cron() in UTC. The newer EventBridge Scheduler accepts the same rate() and cron() syntax plus a time zone per schedule, a start and end date, and one-time at() schedules. Both have a minimum granularity of one minute.

When converting a crontab schedule, add the year field, replace the unconstrained day field with ?, and shift numeric weekdays by one — or paste it into the converter on this page, which does all three.

faq.q: Should I use rate() or cron() for every 5 minutes?
faq.a: Either works. rate(5 minutes) is simpler; cron(0/5 * * * ? *) aligns the runs to :00, :05, :10 on the clock.

faq.q: Why is my rate(1 minutes) expression invalid?
faq.a: For a value of 1, the unit must be singular: rate(1 minute), rate(1 hour), rate(1 day).

faq.q: What is the year field for?
faq.a: It restricts a rule to certain years, for example cron(0 9 1 1 ? 2027) for once on 1 January 2027. Use * for every year.

faq.q: Can EventBridge cron use my local time zone?
faq.a: Rules use UTC only. EventBridge Scheduler lets you set an IANA time zone such as Europe/Berlin on each schedule.
